notes:
I've organised these notes by verse. My research was cut short by tool limits, so some parts are thin and are listed at the end. I found no clear Protestant denominational split on this chapter. Where commentators from different traditions read a phrase differently, I've labelled them by tradition.

---

**vv. 1–4 (bringing the firstfruits)**

- **v. 1:** Israel is still camped on the plains of Moab, so these instructions are for after the people have settled in the land. Precept Austin notes that the land is stressed as a gift and an inheritance, pointing back to God's promise to Abraham. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary
- **v. 1:** Utley (bible.org) calls "gives you as an inheritance" a way of speaking about Israel being chosen. All land belongs to God, he says, and He could remove a disobedient Israel from it, but would still show mercy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary
- **v. 2, one-off or yearly?** Commentators differ. Ryrie thinks this offering was probably made only once, after the first harvest in the land. He adds there was also a yearly firstfruits offering, a pledge of the full harvest to come. Coakley (Moody) also sees it as a one-time offering for the first generation. Guzik agrees it was a special offering, separate from the regular firstfruits of Numbers 18:12. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/
- **v. 2:** Utley says the amount isn't fixed, only that it fit in a basket. The offering was a picture of God owning the whole crop, the same idea behind the firstborn, the tithe, the Sabbath and the Jubilee. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary
- **v. 2, "the place he will choose":** The NET note (quoted on Precept Austin) says this phrase is a roundabout way of naming the central sanctuary: first the tabernacle, later the temple in Jerusalem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary
- **v. 2, older commentators:** One older commentator on StudyLight says the offering kept God's kindness in constant memory. Because God being the author of all their blessings, the first-fruits of the land were consecrated to him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/26-2.html
- **v. 2, background:** The IVP Bible Background Commentary links firstfruits offerings in the ancient Near East to the hope of fertility. It notes that Sennacherib of Assyria even demanded firstfruits from conquered peoples for Assyria's gods. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary
- **v. 3:** The priest is not necessarily the high priest. The first words of the confession thank God for keeping His promise to Abraham about the land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary
- **v. 3, text note:** The NET note says some Greek (Septuagint) manuscripts read "my God" instead of "your God". It thinks this fits the context better, and the Hebrew may reflect a copying slip. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary
- **v. 4:** Guzik says the offering gave God first place, and he quotes Thompson: it was Yahweh—not Baal—who provided the harvest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/
- **v. 4 and v. 10, priest or worshipper?** Verse 4 has the priest set the basket down; verse 10 has the worshipper do it. Kalland says these don't conflict: one passage says a person did something, and another names who actually carried it out for him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary

**vv. 5–10 (the confession)**

- **v. 5, who is "my father"?** The traditional reading is Jacob. He is called an Aramean (a "Syrian" in the KJV) because of his long residence in Mesopotamia (Genesis 29-31.), whence Abraham had originally come (Genesis 11:31), and because there the family of which he was the head was founded (Pulpit Commentary). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/26-5.htm
- **v. 5, "wandering" or "perishing"?** The Hebrew verb can mean both. The Pulpit Commentary says "ready to perish" is a fair rendering, because the verb also means to be lost or in danger of perishing. NIDOTTE (a Hebrew word dictionary) says it is hard to decide between the two. One article cited by Precept Austin, drawing on cuneiform parallels, argues for "A starving Aramean." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/26-5.htm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary
- **v. 5, older translations:** Some read the verse quite differently. The Targum, Vulgate, Luther, etc., have, "The Aramaean (i.e. Laban) oppressed my father;" The LXX., Συρίαν ἀπέλιπεν ὁ πατήρ μου ("My father left Syria"). The Pulpit Commentary thinks these renderings either follow a different text or try to soften how humbling the description is. Keil and Delitzsch reject the "Laban" reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/26-5.htm
- **v. 5, a Methodist teacher:** Adam Clarke takes "ready to perish" to mean the harsh treatment and hard work Jacob suffered under Laban, which may often have put his life at risk. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/ (Clarke also records the Vulgate rendering "A Syrian persecuted my father": https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/26-5.html)
- **v. 5, humility:** Clarke (quoted by Guzik) says Israel had to remember its lowly past that they might be ever kept humble and dependent. Joe Holland (Ligonier, Reformed) argues God commanded worship to begin from a deep humility, and that the verse ultimately points to Christ as the one in whom faith rests. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/ ; https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/when-your-dad-wandering-aramean
- **v. 5, "sojourned":** Guzik notes the 400 years in Egypt are called only a "sojourn" in God's plan. Believers shouldn't let a season of trial define their whole life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/
- **v. 5, "few in number":** Guzik thinks God sent the family to Egypt so it could grow without being absorbed into the Canaanites. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/
- **vv. 6–9:** I found no separate notes for these verses. Guzik treats them within verses 5–10 as a summary of Israel's history from Jacob through slavery to the Exodus and the land. The Bible Hub summary notes that verse 8 stresses God's power over oppression. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/ ; https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/26.htm
- **v. 10:** Guzik says this first giving was a fitting thank-you, and that any giving done with the right heart is worship. He quotes Merrill: settled farming would prove God had kept His word, and the farmer brought firstfruits in tribute to the Lord's electing and saving grace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/

**v. 11 (rejoicing)**

- Guzik: receiving from God and giving back should make His people rejoice, and their gratitude should overflow in generosity to the Levite and the foreigner. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/
- Utley says worship should be joyful, and reverence shouldn't be equated with silence and gloom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-26-commentary

**vv. 12–15 (the third-year tithe)**

- **v. 12:** Guzik: Israel tithed every year, but every third year the tithe was shared with the needy. It was handled by local Levites rather than taken to the sanctuary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/
- **v. 12:** The Bridgeway Bible Commentary adds that this meant the priests didn't oversee how this tithe was distributed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/26-2.html
- **v. 13, boasting?** Guzik quotes Trapp: the declaration isn't Pharisee-style boasting or a claim to merit, but a public statement of full obedience. A Geneva-style note on Bible Hub qualifies "I have done…" as As far as my sinful nature would allow, citing Psalm 14:3 and Romans 3:10. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/26-14.htm
- **v. 14, "in mourning":** Readings vary:
  - Keil, the Pulpit Commentary and Barnes: ritual uncleanness from contact with death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/26-14.htm
  - Calvin (Reformed): most interpreters take it to mean that even in poverty the people had not touched the holy things. He accepts that reading, though he thinks "mourning" could also mean a guilty conscience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/26-14.html
  - Wesley (Methodist): not giving grudgingly, but eating and feasting cheerfully with the poor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-26.html
- **v. 14, "for the dead":** Readings vary:
  - Barnes, the Pulpit Commentary and Wesley: funeral costs or meals for mourners, which would make holy food unclean. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/26-14.htm
  - Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: offerings to idols, which Clarke calls generally a dead man whom superstition and ignorance had deified. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/26-14.html
  - Matthew Henry: honouring dead gods, or hoping to help dead friends. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_026.cfm
  - Utley (modern) and many scholars: Canaanite worship of ancestors. https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-26
  - Kalland (quoted by Guzik): Egyptian and Canaanite practice of putting food in graves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/
  - Gill reports that Jewish interpreters understood it as buying coffins or grave clothes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/26-14.html
- **v. 14, Catholic translation:** The Douay-Rheims renders the phrase as "nor spent any thing of them in funerals." https://biblehub.com/catholic/deuteronomy/26-14.htm
- **v. 15:** Guzik says right giving expects that God will bless in return. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/

**vv. 16–19 (the covenant declared)**

- **v. 16:** Guzik notes that most often we don't need more teaching about God's law but encouragement to actually do it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/
- **v. 17:** Barnes reads "avouched" literally as "made to say": by promising, Israel gave the Lord occasion to say He is their God. Matthew Henry: God is Israel's God by right, and now also by thy own consent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/26-17.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_026.cfm
- **v. 18, conditional promise or grace?** Here there is a real difference of emphasis. Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) says the promise was on condition of their obedience to him. Matthew Poole explains why keeping the commands is listed as God's act: we obey only because His grace gives us the will and power to (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Clarke (Methodist) says God shows publicly that Israel is His people by the blessings He pours on them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/26-18.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/26-18.htm
- **v. 18, the Targums:** Gill reports that the Targums (ancient Aramaic paraphrases) read verses 17–18 as Israel making the Lord its King, that is, a theocracy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/26-18.html
- **vv. 18–19, "special people":** Guzik says this doesn't mean every Israelite was right with God, which came only through personal faith. It means Israel has a key role in God's plan, and its exaltation depended on obedience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-26/

**Debated modern teaching (firstfruits and prosperity; vv. 2, 10)**

- Monergism (Reformed) criticises Paula White for misuse of old-covenant first-fruits, feast, priesthood, and atonement texts as principles governing Christian blessing. It argues these laws belonged to Israel's land and priesthood, which Christ fulfilled, so the New Testament nowhere commands Christians to give "first-fruits" offerings. https://www.monergism.com/paula-white
- By contrast, Ligonier's devotional on Proverbs 3:9–10 does apply the principle to Christians: give to God first, not after spending on yourself. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/honoring-god-your-wealth

**Not found:** articles from bibleodyssey.org; the NET notes for verses 5–19 (the page didn't load, so I only have the two notes quoted on Precept Austin); Catholic or Orthodox commentary from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org (apart from the Douay and Vulgate translations above); and dedicated Lutheran or Pentecostal discussion of this chapter.
